Project Page: https://lensfamily.github.io/LensErase/ Abstract We introduce LensErase , a general-purpose mask-based Erase Anything foundation model designed to cover a broad spectrum of real-world erase scenarios. LensErase supports diverse objects, visual text, watermarks, associated visual effects, multiple-object removal, and a wide range of object scales, aspect ratios, and image resolutions. First, to enable such broad coverage, we construct LensErase-100M , a large-scale dataset containing 101.07 101.07 million paired source–mask–target examples spanning diverse erase scenarios. Second, we pretrain LensErase from the text-to-image model Lens , adapting its strong generative prior to mask-based erasing. To efficiently incorporate the source image and erase mask, we propose Mask-Aware RoPE , a 3D rotary positional encoding that directly injects mask information into the source-image tokens without introducing a separate mask token sequence. Finally, we refine the model through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with contract-guided, region-aware rewards, and apply TraceFusion at inference to preserve high-fidelity content outside the effective edit region. Across six public benchmarks and the proposed LensErase-Bench , LensErase achieves substantial improvements under both reference-based objective metrics and reference-free VLM evaluation. We hope LensErase can serve as a foundational model for erase-related applications and systems. Introduction Object erasing [ 63 , 25 , 75 ] is a fundamental image-editing capability with broad applications in photography, content creation, graphic design, and automated visual-production pipelines. Given an input image and a user-specified region, an ideal erase model should understand what the user intends to remove, eliminate all visual evidence associated with the target, and plausibly reconstruct content that is geometrically, semantically, and visually consistent with the surrounding scene, while preserving the remainder of the image. However, building a single erase model that works reliably across the diverse requests encountered in real-world applications remains challenging. Handling targets across a wide range of spatial scales , from tiny objects occupying less than 1 % 1\% of an image to dominant foreground objects covering nearly half of the scene, requires both precise local editing and reconstruction of large missing regions. Erasing diverse target types poses distinct reconstruction challenges: text and logos require removing fine strokes without damaging nearby details, while translucent watermarks require recovering underlying content from blended pixels. Multi-object removal requires clearing every selected instance while maintaining scene consistency across spatially separated edits. Removing associated visual effects , such as reflections and shadows, requires recognizing and removing target-dependent changes that may extend beyond the selection mask [ 63 , 75 ] . We introduce LensErase , a general-purpose Erase Anything model conditioned only on a source image and an erase mask. To enable broad coverage, we construct LensErase-100M , a large-scale dataset containing 101.07 101.07 million paired training examples, each consisting of a source image, an erase mask, and a target image. LensErase-100M is two to three orders of magnitude larger than representative object-removal datasets, which contain approximately 100 100 K– 1 1 M training examples [ 62 , 31 , 25 ] . Beyond scale, LensErase-100M is systematically constructed to cover diverse object categories, visual text, watermark types, object scales, image resolutions, and multi-object settings. We use domain-specific construction and validation pipelines to ensure reliable source–target supervision. General Data is constructed by inserting scene-compatible objects into clean real-world images and reversing the pairs, preserving the original images as removal targets. Specialized pipelines use alpha compositing for watermarks, layer rendering for posters, verified teacher edits for visual text, and foreground compositing for large objects. LensErase builds upon a pretrained text-to-image model, Lens [ 9 ] , leveraging its strong generative prior to reconstruct realistic and contextually coherent content in erased regions. Since both the condition and output are visual, we initialize both the image branch and condition branch from the pretrained Lens image branch. The condition branch receives the intact source image, allowing the model to identify the target and its associated effects, such as shadows and reflections. Mask-Aware RoPE injects region identity directly into the source-image tokens without introducing a separate mask token sequence. Region-weighted supervision further emphasizes the intended edit during pretraining, producing LensErase-Base . We then refine the model through supervised fine-tuning on curated high-quality, high-resolution data. While large-scale supervised training equips the model with broad erase capabilities, removal quality can still vary across stochastic samples for the same input. Some outputs achieve complete and clean removal, while others may leave target fragments or residual effects, or alter neighboring content. We therefore further optimize the supervised model with reinforcement learning (RL) using DiffusionNFT [ 76 ] . Region-aware rewards encourage complete removal, plausible reconstruction, and preservation of non-target content. At inference, TraceFusion estimates the effective edit region from the selection mask and source–output residuals, and selectively restores the source image outside this region to improve fidelity. Together, RL and TraceFusion yield LensErase , combining reliable removal with high-fidelity preservation. We also introduce LensErase-Bench , a benchmark of 500 removal cases spanning natural images, posters, watermarks, and visual text. Its reference-free visual evaluation assesses removal correctness, reconstruction quality, content preservation and visual cleanliness, complementing reference-based metrics when multiple plausible reconstructions exist. We evaluate LensErase against 12 existing methods on LensErase-Bench and six public benchmarks. LensErase achieves substantial gains under both reference-based objective metrics and reference-free VLM evaluation, demonstrating strong and consistent performance across diverse erase scenarios. We aim for LensErase to serve as a general-purpose erase model for diverse visual-generation and editing systems. Data Pre-Training Data: LensErase-100M We construct LensErase-100M , a large-scale pre-training dataset comprising 101.07M data triplets, where each triplet is represented as ( I input , I output , M ) (I_{\text{input}},I_{\text{output}},M) , denoting the input image, erased target image, and corresponding erase mask, respectively. LensErase-100M covers five major data categories: General Data (77.6M), Watermark Data (9.99M), Large-Mask Data (4.02M), Visual Text Data (1.44M), and Poster Data (8.02M). We construct general object-removal pairs by adding an object to a real image and reversing the pair. We observe that general-purpose editing models perform addition more reliably than removal, which often leaves target remnants, changes unrelated backgrounds, or produces blurry fills and artifacts. Using the original real image as the clean target grounds supervision in the real-image distribution and encourages realistic outputs. The construction pipeline is as follows. 1. Object Taxonomy. We define a hierarchical taxonomy with 15 coarse categories (e.g., Animal, Furniture, and Infrastructure), each further divided into multiple fine-grained object classes. 2. Instruction Generation. We first build an image-caption pool 𝒟 = ( I , T ) \mathcal{D}={(I,T)} . For each sample, we sample three distinct coarse categories. Given ( I , T ) (I,T) and the three sampled categories, GPT-4.1 [ 40 ] is instructed to select an object that is absent from I I , belongs to one of these categories, and can be naturally inserted into the scene. It outputs the corresponding coarse category, object class, and an insertion instruction P P (e.g., “add a dog on the grass”). 3. Dynamic Balancing. Sampling is dynamically adjusted according to accumulated category/object statistics. Over-represented categories or object classes are excluded from subsequent sampling to maintain data diversity and balance. 4. Object Insertion. Given the original image I I and insertion instruction P P , we use an off-the-shelf image editing model G add G_{\mathrm{add}} to synthesize an image with the target object inserted. We use the inserted image as the input to the erase model, I input = G add ​ ( I , P ) I_{\text{input}}=G_{\mathrm{add}}(I,P) , and the original image as the desired erase output, I output = I I_{\text{output}}=I . 5. Coarse-to-Fine Mask Generation. We threshold low-frequency DCT and DINOv3 [ 52 ] feature differences between I input I_{\text{input}} and I output I_{\text{output}} to obtain complementary binary change maps. Their union defines a high-recall change region, while the interior of their overlap provides reliable positive-point candidates. Negative points are sampled outside the union. SAM2 [ 48 ] uses these prompts to produce the final object-selection mask M M . Watermark Data. We construct watermark-removal data through the following pipeline. 1. Watermark Collection. We collect a diverse set of commonly seen watermark patterns in real-world images, including logo watermarks, text watermarks, repeated watermarks, diagonal cross-image watermarks, stripe-style watermarks, and small corner marks. 2. Watermark Synthesis. For each clean image, we randomly select a watermark asset or text. We then synthesize the watermark with randomized font, color, position, scale, rotation, opacity, stroke, and overall layout to cover diverse real-world watermark appearances. 3. Triplet Construction. Since the watermark is rendered programmatically, we do not estimate the mask from image differences. We treat the watermarked image as the erase-model input, the clean image as the erase target, and the rendered region as the mask, i.e., I input I_{\text{input}} is the synthesized watermarked image, I output I_{\text{output}} is the original clean image, and M M is the watermark mask. Large-Mask Data. We observe that large-mask samples are relatively under-represented in the General Data, since current general-purpose editing models struggle to insert very large objects naturally into a scene through prompting alone without occluding existing objects. We therefore construct an additional large-mask subset using a controllable copy-paste pipeline. 1. Foreground Generation. We define a foreground-object taxonomy containing 25 coarse categories and approximately 2.5K fine-grained classes. We randomly select a fine-grained class and generate a matching object on a white background using an image generation model. We then apply BiRefNet [ 77 ] to extract the foreground object and its alpha mask. 2. Copy-Paste. We sample a clean background image I I and apply YOLOE [ 60 ] to detect existing objects in the scene. The generated foreground is then scaled to occupy a relatively large image region and pasted preferentially into areas that do not overlap with detected objects. 3. Triplet Construction. We use the composite image after copy-paste as the erase-model input I input I_{\text{input}} , the original background image as the clean target I output I_{\text{output}} , and the transformed foreground alpha mask as the erase mask M M . Visual Text Data. We construct visual-text removal data through the following pipeline. 1. Text Detection. Given an image I I containing visual text, we first apply PaddleOCR [ 14 ] to detect text regions and their bounding boxes. 2. Text Editing. We use an image editing model with a prompt that instructs it to erase text while preserving its carriers and other scene content, producing a teacher-edited image I ~ \tilde{I} . 3. Candidate Removal Identification. We run PaddleOCR again on I ~ \tilde{I} and compare the OCR results before and after editing. Text regions detected in I I but no longer matched in I ~ \tilde{I} are treated as candidate removal regions. We further use SSIM to exclude candidates that exhibit insufficient structural change despite the OCR mismatch. 4. Poisson Blending. We randomly select a subset of eligible text groups and blend the corresponding regions from I ~ \tilde{I} into the original image I I , preserving unselected text and surrounding content. Poisson blending [ 44 ] reduces color seams introduced by the editing model. 5. Triplet Construction. We use the original image with text as the erase-model input, i.e., I input = I I_{\text{input}}=I . The Poisson-blended image is used as the target I output I_{\text{output}} , and the union of the selected text regions, with a small dilation, forms the mask M M . The resulting triplets are accepted as valid removal pairs after the quality filtering detailed in Appendix B.1.4 . Poster Data. We construct poster-element removal data by modeling a poster as a structured set of layers with explicit z-order. 1. Canvas and Layout Sampling. We first sample a canvas from either a natural image or a design background, and randomly choose a canvas aspect ratio and a layout template. 2. Element Generation. We populate each poster with approximately 4–9 elements. The element types include title, subtitle, paragraph, label, price, date, URL, basic shape, decorative strip, logo, QR code, and chart. For each element, we randomly sample its content and attributes, including font, language, color, opacity, and other style parameters. 3. Structured Layer Composition. All elements are organized as a structured layer set with explicit z-order, which determines their spatial arrangement and mutual occlusion. Under a fixed background, layout, and layer configuration, we render the complete poster. 4. Element Deletion. We randomly remove a subset of elements while keeping the same background, layout, and remaining layer states unchanged, and render the edited poster after deletion. 5. Triplet Construction. We use the complete poster as the erase-model input I input I_{\text{input}} , the poster after deleting the selected elements as the target image I output I_{\text{output}} , and the visible regions of the removed elements as the mask M M . The mask is determined according to the z-order of the layered poster, so that only the actually visible pixels of the removed elements are included. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) Data SFT Data. We follow the pretraining pipelines in Section 2.1 , prioritizing high-resolution images. All candidate triplets undergo GPT-5.6 Sol [ 41 ] screening for mask validity, edit correctness, non-target preservation, and reconstruction quality (Appendix B.2 ). We do not include Large-Mask Data in SFT, as these examples are synthetically generated and are mainly used to improve the coverage of large-mask cases during pre-training. For Poster Data, instead of using the synthetic generation pipeline adopted during pre-training, we collect high-quality poster examples designed by professional designers, providing more realistic layouts, typography, and visual compositions. The SFT set contains 140K examples: 80K General Data, 20K Watermark Data, 20K Visual Text Data, and 20K Poster Data. RL Data. We curate 19K image–mask tasks using source images disjoint from SFT. General Data contains 8K difficulty-filtered Hard/Extreme cases and 5K targeted supplements. Manual analysis of LensErase-SFT failures guides collection of new images with similar challenges. For annotated General Data tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol [ 41 ] localizes objects, including those with associated effects. SAM2 converts their bounding boxes into masks. GPT then assesses difficulty from the validated source–mask pairs without observing erase-model outputs. Poster, Watermark, and Visual Text contribute 2K tasks each through high-resolution layered removal, controlled synthesis, and screened text removal with text-centered cropping, respectively. The model receives only I input I_{\text{input}} and M M . General Data requires no paired target. Poster and Watermark use deterministic clean references, whereas Visual Text uses verified weak references for rewards. Appendix B.3 details the pipelines. Evaluation Dataset: LensErase-Bench LensErase-Bench. Most existing object-removal benchmarks evaluate outputs against paired reference images obtained through synthesis or real-world capture. Synthesized references may contain artifacts, while separately captured references may differ in lighting or scene details. Since object removal also admits multiple valid outcomes, agreement with a single reference may not fully reflect removal quality. To complement reference-based metrics, we introduce LensErase-Bench , a benchmark of 500 carefully curated removal cases evaluated without paired ground-truth target images. A VLM evaluates each output against the source image and selection mask. The Poster subset uses layered designs from Crello [ 66 ] . We also include image–mask pairs selected from existing segmentation datasets [ 47 , 15 , 64 ] . We normalize the selected images to a shorter side above 512 pixels and a longer side below 2048 pixels while preserving aspect ratio. We carefully curate the benchmark to provide balanced coverage across multiple dimensions, including application scenarios, mask area ratio, image resolution, selected-target count, and erase difficulty. These factors are jointly considered to ensure that LensErase-Bench is both diverse and representative of practical applications. Each evaluation sample consists of an input image I input I_{\text{input}} and an erase mask M M . Appendix C details the selection constraints and distributions. Evaluation Metrics. We use GPT-5.6 Sol [ 41 ] as the VLM judge to evaluate each output against the input image and selection mask along four dimensions: Removal , the completeness of removing selected targets and their associated effects; Inpainting , plausible completion consistent with the surrounding context; Preservation , retention of non-target content; and Cleanliness , absence of artifacts and unrelated additions. Each dimension receives an integer rating from 0 0 to 4 4 , rescaled to 0 0 – 100 100 for reporting. Overall weights these dimensions by 40 % 40\% , 20 % 20\% , 20 % 20\% , and 20 % 20\% , respectively. We additionally report the High-Fidelity Removal Rate ( HiFi Removal , %), the percentage of all valid cases that achieve complete removal while meeting the quality requirements for inpainting, preservation, and visual cleanliness. Specifically, a case is successful when Removal = 4 =4 and Inpainting, Preservation, and Cleanliness are all ≥ 3 \geq 3 on the original 0 0 – 4 4 scale. Mean scores are computed over all valid cases with equal weight per image. Detailed scoring rules and the evaluation protocol are provided in Appendix C.2 . We initialize LensErase from Lens [ 9 ] , a text-to-image model whose MMDiT backbone contains a condition branch for the text modality and an image branch for the visual modality. LensErase follows the same backbone architecture, but both branches are initialized from the pretrained image branch of Lens. This is because, in the erase task, the condition input, including the mask M M and source image features, is also visual. Figure 3 illustrates the architecture of LensErase: the image branch processes the noisy target latent, while the condition branch processes the source latent. The erase mask M M , with 1 denoting the masked region and 0 the unmasked region, is incorporated into the condition branch through the proposed Mask-Aware RoPE with negligible computational overhead. We retain the complete source image, including the selected region. The selected object’s appearance and location help identify associated shadows and reflections, while semi-transparent overlays retain useful information about the underlying background.
